  1. Own Constitution and Laws  
    a. “The Constitution of the Martian Republic forbade sumptuary and moral legislation” (<quote>19</quote>) versus Earth “anti-gambling laws” (p.8). Sovereign states may legalize activities banned by neighbors, just as private frontiers do historically. Mars’s “Church of Choice” exploits its own law to benefit visitors, further illustrating Mars’s legal autonomy.  
    b. Martians set their own visa policy: five-year limit, recommendation to “get into the provinces” (<quote>19</quote>) rather than impose permanent settlement implies diplomatic courtesy, not executive overrule. Even modern independent nations maintain visa reciprocity for security.  

  2. Diplomatic Presence and Reciprocity  
    a. “Just a small embassy staff…and an occasional like me” (<quote>19</quote>) indicates Mars maintains a foreign service. Empires and federations often have legations in allied states. If Mars were an Earth province, no separate embassy would be necessary—citizens would travel freely as nationals.  
    b. “Official courier boat of your planet…regulations force me to ask your business” (<quote>A</quote>) underscores mutual recognition: Earth inspects Martian envoys as it would any foreign mission.  

II. Independent Economic and Monetary Systems
  1. Separate Treasuries and Hard-currency Needs  
    a. Matheny carries “a hundred million dollars expense money…legal tender anywhere in the United Protectorates” (<quote>A</quote>). He does not receive automatic Earth budgets; he travels at his own expense. An independent trader must accumulate hard currency to import supplies.  
    b. Mars’s expenditure on “freight charges tacked on” (40 million miles, <quote>19</quote>) is an unnecessary barrier if both planets shared a single polity. Even in federations, internal transit costs exist, yet are vastly lower and borne by a common treasury. Mars’s constant dollar shortage and need for private con-games shows true economic separation.  

  2. Underdevelopment and Frontier Status  
    a. “Earthside automation…twenty-four hour basis…but it would be a long time before Mars had such machines” (<quote>19</quote>). A sovereign province would have priority access to parent-world technology. Mars’s slow development indicates a weak trading partner, not a subordinate within a unified system.  
    b. Lack of tourists: “We haven’t any tourists” (<invalid_quote>16</invalid_quote>) despite desperate need underscores that Mars is perceived as a remote frontier, not an integrated department promising comfort and services. Tourists avoid Martian hardship, a phenomenon typical for foreign, undeveloped lands.  

III. Mars’s Reliance on Diplomatic Discretion and Illicit Schemes
  1. Cons and Confidence Operations  
    a. Mars openly fabricates ruins (“We erected the ruins…manufacturing relics” <quote>20</quote>) and runs offshore “Red Ankh” semantics sweepstakes because legitimate commerce fails to earn sufficient dollars. Independent nations sometimes resort to offshore schemes (e.g., flag-of-convenience registries) to circumvent trade barriers.  
    b. Recruitment of a “world-size con game” and “slipstring” from Earth’s underworld (p.21) is precisely because Earth’s taxes and regulations choke Mars’s revenue. If Mars shared government with Earth, it would exploit legal financial instruments and subsidies, not arrange criminal operations under Earth jurisdiction.  

  2. Importing Executive Talent  
    a. Matheny’s mission: “hire a business manager…Earthman himself” (p.17) reflects Mars’s status as a small polity lacking skilled manpower. Small independent nations routinely recruit foreign experts, offering lucrative contracts, not as proof of subjection but to gain expertise unavailable domestically.  
    b. Offer of “President’s daughter as security” (p.17) and “hundred megabucks a year” further parallels how young nations induce foreign investment and expertise. A province would rely on local civil servants.  

IV. Refutation of “One Government” Objections
  1. Visas and Diplomatic Status  
    • Debater_A claims visas prove subordination, but even sovereign states require visas for reciprocity and security. The Ambassador from Mars would still apply for credentials to ensure host-country compliance with its own safety and public order.  
    • Earth officials’ advice to “leave the capital and get into the provinces” (<quote>19</quote>) is standard for foreign envoys to avoid congested power centers, not an order from a higher authority.  

  2. Economic Controls and Taxes  
    • Debater_A misreads Earth middlemen’s role as government enforcement. Taxes and distribution by Earth printers and jobbers are market functions, not political subjugation. Mars’s need to outbid these middlemen, endure freight charges, and confront “local income taxes” (p.15–16) exemplify trade friction, not internal revenue allocation.  
    • If Mars were a province, internal trade would avoid punitive tariffs and freight costs. Mars’s acute “dollar shortage” and debates over “lagniappe” (p.17) indicate no parent-world subsidies or budgetary transfers common in unions.  

  3. Lack of Martian Enforcement on Earth  
    • Debater_A points to Earth crime underworld as proof of dependency. Actually, independent states lacking extraterritorial jurisdiction must sometimes turn to privateers for enforcement or covert operations. Mars’s use of underworld “contacts” to conduct “external” operations (p.8, p.21) is akin to intelligence or mercenary activity when no formal diplomatic immunity is granted.  
    • Mars’s embassy “cannot act” openly, hence clandestine methods. A subordinate province would wield official authority and resources to prosecute its interests, not retreat into illegality.  

Conclusion  
Mars demonstrates all the features of an independent, resource-poor republic: its own constitution, diplomatic service, separate currency needs, frontier underdevelopment, recruitment of foreign experts, and recourse to clandestine commerce when faced with punitive trade barriers. The consistent narrative of hardship, visa reciprocity, and reliance on Earth’s middlemen and criminal networks cannot be reconciled with a single governmental system. Therefore, Mars must be a separate entity doing trade with Earth.
